translations.text: Thus Alfred, king of the West Saxons, told us an old story. He displayed his skill, the craft of the poet.

He had a great desire to tell songs to these people, mirth to men, sayings of many kinds, so that boredom would not drive away the self-satisfied man, who cares little for such things because of his pride.
I must speak further, take up the song, and tell men counsel that is known among the people. Let whoever will, listen!

It was long ago that the Goths came from the east, out of Scythia, bearing shields. In a great host they overran many a nation's land, and in the south they established two victorious peoples. The kingdom of the Goths grew year by year.
They had two kings of their own kin, Radagaisus and Alaric. They prospered in power.
Then many a Goth was drawn over the Alps, full of boasting and eager for battle, for war between peoples. The banner swirled, bright on its staff.

The warriors, the shield-fighters, meant to overrun all Italy. And they did it, all the way from the Alps to the famous shore where Sicily, a great island in the sea-streams, makes its homeland renowned.

Then the kingdom of the Romans was conquered, the finest of cities was sacked, and Rome was laid open to the warriors. Radagaisus and Alaric went into the stronghold. The emperor fled with the princes away to the Greeks.

Then the wretched survivors could not hold out against the Goths in battle. The guardians of the homeland gave up, against their will, the treasures of their forefathers, and swore holy oaths. Either way there was woe.
Yet the young men's hearts were with the Greeks, if they had dared to follow a leader of the people.
Things stood that way for a time. The people had been conquered for many winters, until fate decreed that thegns and nobles should obey Theodoric.
The army's leader was bound to Christ; the king himself received the rite of baptism. All the children of the Romans rejoiced and quickly sought peace with him.
He firmly promised them that they could keep each of their ancient rights with honour in the wealthy city, for as long as God wished him to hold power over the Goths. He broke that whole promise.
To that prince the heresy of Arius was dearer than the law of the Lord.
He ordered John, the good pope, to be beheaded. That was no noble deed.
Besides that, the Goth committed countless other crimes against every good man.
Then in the city of Rome there was a certain powerful man who had been raised up as a leader. He was dear to his lord while the Greeks held the royal throne.
He was a righteous man. For a long time afterward there was no better giver of treasure among the Romans.
He was wise in the ways of the world, eager for honours, a man learned in books. The hero who won that fame was called Boethius.

At all times he kept in mind the evil and insult that foreign kings had shown him. He was loyal to the Greeks. He remembered the honours and ancient rights, the love and favours, that his ancestors had long enjoyed among them.
Then he began to think cunningly and earnestly about how he might bring the Greeks back there, so that the emperor might once again hold power over them.

He secretly sent letters to the old lords. By the Lord and by their old loyalty he begged them to come back to them in the city, to let the Greek counsellors govern the Romans, and to let the people have their rights.
When Theodoric the Amaling learned of that plan, he seized the thegn and ordered his companions to hold the warrior fast.
His mind was fierce, and he feared the nobleman. He ordered him to be locked inside a prison cell.
Then Boethius's mind was greatly troubled. For a long time before, he had enjoyed splendour under the heavens, so he could bear that time all the worse when it came on him so harshly.
Then the nobleman was in despair. He expected no mercy and could think of no comfort in that prison. Instead he fell face down to the floor, stretched out, and spoke many words, deeply despondent:
He did not expect ever to come out of those fetters. He called to the Lord in a mournful voice and sang this song:
"Lo, once I gladly sang many songs in happy times. Now, sighing, worn out with weeping, a sad exile, I must sing words of sorrow.
This sighing, this sobbing, has hindered me, so that I cannot compose songs as beautifully, though I once composed many true sayings when I was happy.
Now I often get familiar words wrong, though in the past I sometimes found unfamiliar ones."

"These worldly fortunes have foolishly led me, blind in almost everything, into this dark hole. They robbed me of counsel and comfort through their faithlessness, though I should always have been able to trust them most. They have bitterly turned their backs on me and taken their joy away from me."
My worldly friends, why would you say or sing that I was a happy man in the world? Those words are not true, now that happiness cannot last for ever.
Alas, in how grim and how bottomless a pit the darkening mind struggles when the strong storms of worldly cares beat upon it,
when, struggling, it abandons its own light, and in woe forgets the eternal joy, and pushes into the darkness of this world, afflicted with sorrows.
This is what has now happened to this mind: it no longer knows any good for itself except grieving over a world grown strange to it. It needs comfort.

Alas, you creator of the bright stars, of heaven and earth! You reign eternally on your high throne. You turn the whole heaven swiftly around, and through your holy might you compel the stars to obey you.
In the same way the sun drives out the darkness of the black nights through your might.

With pale light the moon tempers the bright stars through the power of your might. Sometimes it also robs the sun of its bright light, when it happens that they must of necessity come so near each other.
Likewise you compel the glorious morning star, which by another name we call the evening star, to watch over the sun's course. Every year he must go ahead of it on its journey.
Lo, you, Father, make the long summer days very hot, and for the winter days you appoint wondrously short hours.
From the south and west you give leaves back to the trees, which the dark storm from the north and east had earlier stripped of every leaf with its more hateful wind.
"Lo, on earth all creatures obey your command, and in the heavens they do the same with heart and strength, except for man alone, who very often acts against your will."
O you eternal and almighty one, creator and ruler of all creatures, have mercy on your wretched offspring of the earth, the race of men, through the power of your might.
Why, eternal God, would you ever have wished that fortune should turn so greatly to the will of evil men?
Very often she harms the innocent.
"Throughout earthly kingdoms evil men sit on high seats and trample the holy under their feet. Men do not know why fate should turn so wrongly."
So bright virtues are hidden here in the world, throughout many cities.

At all times the unrighteous hold in contempt those who are wiser in righteousness than they are and worthier to rule. That false deceit stays covered with tricks for a long time. Here in the world, false oaths do no harm to men now.
If you now, Ruler, will not steer fate, but let it sink into its own will, then I know that worldly men across the surface of the earth will fall into doubt, except for a few.

Alas, my Lord, you who look over all the world's creatures, look now on mankind with mild eyes, now that they struggle and toil here among the many waves of the world, the wretched dwellers on earth. Have mercy on them now.
You can see this clearly from the sun, and from every other star that shines brightest over the dwellings of men.
If a dark cloud hangs in front of them, they cannot send out so bright a beam until the thick mist grows thinner.
So too the south wind often grimly stirs up the calm sea, grey and clear as glass, when great waves churn together and stir up the whale's sea. Then the sea that before looked so glad is rough.

Just as a spring often wells up, cool and clear, from a grey cliff and flows smoothly and straight, running toward its home, until a great stone from the mountain falls into it and lies in its middle, rolled down from the crag.
Afterwards it is split in two. The clear water is made muddy, the stream is mixed up, and the brook is turned from its right course and flows apart into rivulets.
so now the darkness of your heart will resist my bright teaching and greatly trouble the thoughts of your mind.
But if you now wish to be able to see the true light clearly, with bright faith, you must give up idle excessive pleasures and useless joy.
You must also give up evil fear of worldly hardships. Nor must you therefore be too despairing, and never let pride weaken you, in case it later brings you to shame through arrogance,
and too uplifted because of carefree worldly prosperity, nor again too feebly despair of any good, when the most adverse of things in the world oppress you and you weigh most heavily upon yourself.
For the mind is always greatly bound with trouble if either of these evils may afflict it and torment it within.
For those two griefs draw together a confusing mist in front of the mind, so that the eternal sun cannot shine through within it because of the dark mists, until they are lessened.
Then Wisdom again unlocked his word-hoard, sang true sayings, and spoke as follows:
When the sun shines most clearly, brightest from heaven, all the other stars over the earth are quickly darkened, because their brightness is nothing to set against the light of the sun.
When the wind beneath the clouds blows gently from the south and west, the flowers of the field quickly grow, glad that they are able to.

But the strong storm, when it comes mightily from the north and east, quickly takes away the beauty of the rose; and the northern tempest also forcibly drives the broad sea, so that, violently stirred up, it beats upon the shores.
Alas, that on earth nothing of steadfast work ever endures in the world!

Then Wisdom began to follow his custom: he sang in words of song, a lay after his discourse, and sang yet some true sayings. He said that he had not heard that any man could set up a firm-roofed hall on a high mountain.
Nor need any man expect to achieve the work of ever mingling wisdom with pride.
Have you ever heard that any man could set a firm hall on hills of sand? Nor can any man build wisdom where worldly greed overspreads the hill.
Bare sand will swallow up rain; so now does the bottomless greed of the powerful for glory and possessions: it drinks the perishing wealth dry, and yet the thirst of the needy one is not cooled.
No man can have a house on a mountain last long, because the swift wind suddenly sweeps upon it.
Nor is sand, any more, a guardian of a house for any man against heavy rain; rather it will fall, the sand will sink away after the rain.

In the same way the minds of all men are greatly shaken and stirred from their place when the strong wind of worldly hardships beneath the clouds afflicts them, or when the fierce rain of some anxiety, a boundless care, disturbs them again.

But he who wishes to possess the eternal, true happiness must strongly flee the beauty of this world, and then build for himself the house of his mind where he can find the stone of humility, immeasurably firm, a ready foundation;

it need not slide apart, though the wind of worldly hardships or the immense rain of cares should shake it, because in that valley of humility the Lord himself dwells, firmly settled, where wisdom ever dwells in remembrance.
Therefore wise men of the world always lead a carefree life without change,
when he despises all earthly goods and also remains untroubled by those evils, and hopes for the eternal things that come afterwards;
then almighty God continually and always keeps him on every side, abiding in the happiness of his own mind through the grace of the Creator, though the wind of worldly hardships greatly afflict him,
and constant care hinder him, when the wind of worldly fortune blows grimly and wrathfully upon him, though anxiety about these worldly fortunes always cruelly torment him.
As soon as Wisdom had clearly set out these words, he began to sing true sayings, and spoke as follows:
Lo, the first age was good for every earth-dweller throughout the surface of the earth, when to each one the fruits of the earth seemed enough. It is not so now!
There were then no wealthy homes throughout the world, nor various foods and drinks, nor indeed did they care for the garments which nobles now regard as most precious.
For none of them existed yet. Seafarers had not seen them and had not heard of them anywhere around.

Lo, they were not greedy for sinful lusts, except so far as they might most moderately follow the nature which Christ shaped for them; and they ate once a day, always at evening, the fruits of the earth, of wood and herbs; they did not drink bright wine from a deep cup at all.
At that time there was no servant who knew how to mix food or drink, water with honey, nor how to sew their garments with silk,

Nor did they adorn fine cloth with cunning crafts, nor did they skilfully build jewelled halls; but they always, at all times, slept outdoors under the shade of trees, and drank the water of streams, of cold springs.
No merchant saw a foreign shore across the sea. People certainly had not heard of fleets of warships, and no man even spoke of battle.
This earth had not yet been stained anywhere with the blood of a man reddened by a sword, nor had earth-dwellers even seen a wounded man under the sun.
After that no one was honoured in the world if people saw that his will was evil among men; he was hateful to everyone.
Oh, if only it were so, or God willed, that now in our times on earth, throughout this wide world, people were like that in every way under the sun!
But it is worse now: this greed has corrupted the mind of every man, so that he cares for nothing more, and it burns, seething, in his mind.
Truly, greed, which has no bottom, smoulders [?] darkly, just like that mountain which the children of men now call Etna.

It burns with sulphur on the island of Sicily, so that people far and wide call it hell-fire, because it is always burning without end, and with its bitter flame it lividly burns up other places around it.
Alas, who was the first money-greedy man in the world, who dug up these fields for gold and for kinds of gems?
Lo, he found dangerous treasures that had been hidden from many in the world, by water or by earth.
Lo, we all know what impious deeds Nero, king of the Romans, did both near and far, when his kingdom was the highest under the heavens, to the ruin of many.
The madness of that bloodthirsty man was known far and wide: fornication, many impious acts, crime and murder, a multitude of misdeeds, the malicious thoughts of an unrighteous man.
He once ordered, for his amusement, the city of the Romans to be burned, which was the native seat of his whole realm.

In his folly he wanted to test whether the fire could blaze as brightly and also as long, and rage as red, as he had heard the Romans say that the brightest of flames had once overspread the city of Troy and burned the longest of any homes under the heavens.
It was no noble deed that he wanted to boast of such sport, since he gained nothing else by it, except that he wanted at least to make his own sole power known over the nations.

It also happened at one time that this same man ordered all the most powerful counsellors of the Romans to be killed, and the noblest by birth among the nobles that he had heard of among the people, and on top of that his own brother and his mother, to be struck down with the edges of swords, with blades.
He killed his wife himself with a sword, and he was always much the happier in his heart when he had committed the greatest of such murders.

He did not worry at all whether the mighty Lord would ever afterward mete out vengeance to wrongdoers according to their deeds; instead the bloodthirsty man remained glad in spirit at deceit and treachery.
Even so, he ruled all this glorious middle-earth, as far as air and water embrace the land and the ocean girds the kingdom of men, the dwelling-places of men, south,
east and west, as far as the northernmost headlands on earth; all of that, every warrior, had to obey Nero, by force or willingly.
When he rose up in boasting, he took as his sport how he afflicted and killed the kings of the earth.

"Do you think that the power of God Almighty could not easily strip that boastful wrongdoer of his kingdom and rob him of his power through his eternal might, or otherwise restrain him from his evil?"
Oh, if he had wished, as he well could have, he might easily have kept himself from that wrong!
Alas, that the lord laid a heavy yoke grievously on the necks of his thanes, of all the men who in his times had to live throughout this transitory world.
Very often he sullied his sword in the blood of innocent nobles. That made it very clear, as we have often said, that power does no good at all if the one who holds it does not wish to do well.

If any man now desires fame and wants to have useless boasting, then I would ask him in words to look about him on every side, to look clearly around, south, east and west, and see how vast the vaults of heaven are around the clouds.
To the wise-minded it can easily seem that this whole earth is immeasurably small compared with the other. To the unwise, however, it may seem vast and firm in its place, to a man without guidance,

A wise man may well feel shame in his mind at his greed for boasting when he most fiercely desires fame, and yet by no means can he spread it beyond these narrow regions of the earth. That is useless boasting!
O you proud ones, why do you always want to bow your necks, of your own will, under that heavy yoke?
Why do you always toil over that useless thing, striving to have fame among the nations, more than you need?
Even if it should now be your fortune that the most distant earth-dwellers, south or north, praise you greatly in many languages, even if someone is noble by high birth and honoured with riches,
[?] and thrive in splendour, precious in riches, death pays no heed to that when the Ruler of the heavens gives it leave. Instead it makes the wealthy man equal to the poor in every respect.
Where now are the bones of the wise Weland, the goldsmith, who was once most famous?
I said "the bones of the wise Weland" because no dweller on earth can lose the skill that Christ lends him.
No one can ever take a wretched man's skill from him, any more easily than any man can turn the sun aside or move this swift sky from its proper course.
Who now knows where the bones of the wise Weland are, under which of the burial mounds the earth covers them?
Where now is the mighty counsellor of the Romans, the bold one we speak of, their commander, who was called by the name Brutus among the citizens?
Where now also is the wise one, eager for honour, the steadfast shepherd of the people, who was a philosopher in every matter, bold and skilful, whose name was Cato?
They passed away long ago. No man knows where they are now.
What remains of them here except fame alone?
That is also too little for such teachers, because those men deserved more in the world.

But now it is worse: everywhere throughout this earth there are men like them who are little spoken of, and some are plainly forgotten altogether, so that fame cannot bring these very famous men forward as well known.
Though you now hope and wish that you may live a long time, what would ever be better for you, or seem better, because of it?
For death spares no one, though it may seem long in coming, once the number of their days is complete, when it has the Lord's leave.
What then does any hero, any man, gain from that glory if eternal death may seize him after this world?
There is one Creator, without any doubt.

He is also the ruler of the world's creatures: of heaven and earth and the deep sea, and of all those that dwell in them, the invisible ones, and likewise of those we look on with our eyes, of all creatures.
He is almighty. All creatures obey him: those that know anything of that service, and likewise those that do not know at all that they are servants of that Lord.
He set for us customs and ways, unchanging for all creatures, and a peace that is always natural to them, when he wished, as he wished, for as long as he wished it to be.
So it shall also remain forever, for the restless creatures of the world can never be made still and turned from the course that the Guardian of the heavens set in order for them all.

The All-Ruler has bridled all creatures with his bridle. He has done both: he has urged them all on and also held them back, so that against the Creator's will they may never fall still, nor move any more strongly than the Lord of victories wishes to slacken his rein for them.
With that bridle he has held fast both heaven and earth and the whole expanse of the seas.

So has the guardian of the heavenly kingdom constrained all creatures with his power that each of them strives against the other, and yet, while striving, they firmly support one another. Each embraces the other from outside, so that they do not slip apart.
Therefore they must always turn back again to the same course that the Father appointed at the beginning, and so become new once more.
So it now changes, the Lord's ancient work, so that the warring, opposed creation keeps a firm peace from then on.
So now fire and water, earth and sea, and many other creatures struggle with one another, equally strongly, throughout this wide world, and yet they can firmly keep their service and fellowship.
It is not only that opposing creatures can so easily be together and always travel together. What is more wonderful is that none of them can exist without the others.
Rather, every creature under heaven must have something opposed to it, so that it dares to restrain its spirit before it grows too great.
The Almighty has set for all creatures the alternation that must now endure: plants grow and leaves turn green, which in autumn fall again and wither.

Winter brings weather that is cold beyond measure, and swift winds. After it comes summer, with warm weather. Lo, the moon lights up the dark night until the sun brings day to men throughout this wide creation.
The same God has set boundaries for earth and for water.

The sea-stream does not dare to spread its dwelling for the race of fishes over the surface of the earth without the Lord's leave. It may never step up over the threshold of the earth, and the ebb-tides may no more pass over the boundaries of the land.
The Ruler of victories, the source of the light of life, lets those ordinances keep their boundaries throughout this glorious creation for as long as he wills.

But when the eternal and almighty one decides to let go the reins, those very bridles with which he bridled all his own work at the beginning (that is, the opposition of every creature, which we try to express by that bridle);
If the Lord lets them slip apart, at once they abandon love and peace and the friendship of that fellowship;

each one strives for its own will, and the creatures of the world contend among themselves until this earth wholly perishes. In the same way the other creatures also come to nothing of themselves afterwards.
But the same God who regulates all things joins many peoples together and gathers them firmly in friendship. He unites married couples and mingles peace and pure love.
So the Craftsman also firmly unites companions, so that they keep their friendship forever after, with undoubting faith and peace in harmony.
O God of victories, this mankind would be greatly blessed if their minds could be set steadfast and put in order by that strong power, just as the other creatures of the world are.
Ah, it would be pleasant among men if it could be so!

Whoever wishes to work fruitful land should first, at once, pull from the field the ferns and thorns and furze as well. These are weeds that everywhere seek to harm the clean wheat, and they must be removed lest the wheat lie in the land without shoots.
This second example is equally useful to everyone: the honeycomb seems to every man half again as sweet if, a little before the drop of honey, he tastes something bitter.
Likewise every man is much the gladder of mild weather if, a little before, storms and the strong wind from the north and east have beset him.
Day would seem pleasing to no one if the dim night had not first brought terror over men.
So to each earth-dweller true happiness always seems the better and the more delightful, the more torments and harsh afflictions he endures here.
You can also much more easily recognize true happiness more clearly in your mind, and afterwards come to know it,
if you first, at once, pull up and uproot false happinesses from your mind, just as the farmer pulls many an evil weed from his field.
Then I tell you that you will clearly be able to recognize true happinesses at once. If you perceive them fully, you will never care for anything beyond them alone.
I wish to make known yet further in songs how the Almighty drives all creatures with his bridles and bends them wherever he wishes with his power, and how wondrously well he regulates their order.
The ruler of the heavens has so constrained all creatures, surrounded them from outside and bound them with his chain, that they cannot manage ever to slip away from him;
Yet every creature of the wide creation strains, leaning and greatly inclined, toward the nature that the King of angels, the Father, firmly appointed for it at the beginning.
So now each thing in the wide creation strives toward that place, except some angels and mankind, of whom far too many among the world's dwellers fight against their nature.
Suppose you now come upon a lion in the land, a winsome creature, well tamed, which greatly loves its master and also fears him every day. If it ever happens that she tastes any blood,
No man need expect that she will keep her tameness well after that event. I think instead that she will pay no attention at all to her new tameness, but will remember the wild ways of her ancestors;
she begins in earnest to tear the chains, to roar, to growl, and first she bites the keeper of her own house, and quickly afterwards every man she can catch.
she will not spare any living creature, neither cattle nor men; she seizes everything she finds.
Wood-birds do the same. Though they are well and thoroughly tamed, if they get into the trees in the middle of the wood, they quickly scorn their teachers, who long before had trained and tamed them.
From then on they gladly live in the trees according to their wild ancestral nature, even if one of their teachers should skilfully offer them the same food with which he had tamed them before.
The twigs seem so pleasant to them that they care nothing for the food; it seems so delightful to them when the forest answers them;
when they hear other birds warbling their notes, they stir up their own voices; all together they ring out a delightful song, and the wood answers them all.

So it is with all trees whose nature it is to grow highest in the wood: though you bend some bough down toward the earth, it goes upward again; as soon as you let the wood go free, it turns back to its nature.
So does the sun also: when it is going down after midday, the sea-candle hurries on its descent and ventures by night on an unknown way, north again and east;
it appears to people and brings the earth-dwellers a bright morning over the sea. It climbs ever upward over mankind until it comes again to where its highest place, its natural home, is.
Just as every creature throughout this wide world strives and hastens with all its might, so it always turns back again with all its might and returns to its own nature when it can.
There is now no creature on earth that does not long to come back to the homeland it came from. That homeland is freedom from care and eternal rest; that is, plainly, almighty God.
There is now no creature on earth that does not turn upon itself, as a wheel does. For it turns in such a way that it comes back to where it was before;
when it has first been turned outward, when it has been turned wholly outward, it must afterwards do again what it did before, and also be what it was before.
What is the rich, greedy man of the world the better for it in his mind, even if he owns much gold and gems and goods of every kind, possessions beyond counting,
and even if a thousand acres had to be ploughed for him every day, and even if this world and this race of men under the sun, south, west and east, were all made subject to his rule?
He may not take any more of those ornaments, those hoarded treasures, away from this world than he brought into it.

Though the wicked, unrighteous King Nero newly arrayed himself wonderfully in beautiful garments, adorned with gold and with gems of every kind, yet in his lifetime every wise man in the world thought him hateful, worthless and full of sin.
Yet the fiend raised up his favourites with honours.

Yet I cannot understand why they should ever be the happier in their minds for that. Even if the most foolish of kings chose them for a while, though they had no virtues, they were none the worthier for it in the eyes of any of the wise.
Though the fool makes him king, how can a man of good judgement explain that he is, or seems, any better for it?

Whoever wishes to have power must first strive to have power over himself inwardly, in his own mind, so that he is never wholly subject to his vices. Let him put out of his mind the many different cares that are useless to him, and let him for a while leave off lamenting his miseries.
Even if all this middle-earth, as the ocean currents surround it, were given to him to possess, as far as an island now lies westernmost out in the ocean,

where there is no night in summer, and no more in winter is the day divided into hours, which is called Thule; even if one man alone now ruled all that island, and also everything from there eastward as far as the Indians;

Though he may now own all that, why is his power any greater if he afterwards has no control over his own mind, and does not earnestly and carefully guard himself, in words and deeds, against the vices we are speaking of?

Lo, all the inhabitants of the earth, the dwellers on the land, had a like beginning. They all came into the world from just two people, a man and a woman, and they all still come into the world alike now, the proud and the lowly.
That is no wonder, because all wise men know that there is one God of all creatures, Lord of mankind, Father and Creator.
He gives the light of the sun from the heavens, and of the moon and these glorious stars.
The merciful Lord created men on earth and joined soul to body at the very beginning; he created people under the clouds, every man, equally noble.
Why then do you ever arrogantly exalt yourselves over other men without cause, since you find no one who is ignoble?
Why do you raise yourselves up because of your noble birth, since the true nobility I am telling you about lies in the mind of every man, and not at all in the flesh of the dwellers on earth?
But now every man who is wholly subject to his vices first abandons the origin of his life, and likewise his own noble birth, and also the Father who created him in the beginning.
For almighty God makes him ignoble, so that from then on he becomes forever ignoble in the world and does not come to glory.
Alas, how much wrong is done by the evil, wrathful desire for adultery, which troubles the mind of nearly every member of the human race completely.
Lo, the wild bee, wise though it is, must perish utterly if it stings anything in anger.
In the same way every soul must afterwards be lost if the body becomes defiled by unlawful intercourse, unless repentance first comes into the person's heart before he departs from here.
Alas, let anyone who will think about it: it is grievous folly, and dangerous to every man, which leads wretched men utterly astray, so that they are quickly led away from the right path.
Will you look in the woods for red gold on green trees?
Yet I know that no wise man looks for it there, because it does not grow there, nor do beautiful gems grow in vineyards.
Why do you not now set your fishing nets on some hill when you want to catch salmon or kipper-salmon? It seems most likely to me that all thoughtful earth-dwellers know that they are not there.
Or would you now go hunting with hounds in the salt sea when you want to seek harts and hinds? You can well conceive that you will seek them in the woods far more often than out at sea.
It is a wonder, as we all know, that people must seek noble gems along the seashore and the riverbanks: white and red, and of every colour.
Indeed, they also know where they must look for river-fish, and for many such worldly riches; eager men, they do that well every year.
But the most wretched thing of all is that the foolish have fallen into error, so blind that they cannot easily recognise in their hearts where the eternal goods, true happiness, are hidden.
Because they never wish to search after them, to seek those blessings. Half-wise, they think that in this passing life they may find true blessings, that is, God himself.

I do not know how I can in any way blame their folly in my mind as strongly as I would like, nor can I tell you so clearly, for they are more wretched, and also more foolish and more unhappy, than I can tell you.
They desire to win wealth and possessions and honour; when they have what their mind seeks, then, so witless, they think that they have true happiness.
O my Lord, you are almighty, great, magnificent, famed for glories, and wonderful to every wise man.
Indeed, you, eternal God, wondrously and well created all creatures, the invisible ones, and in the same way you gently rule the bright visible creatures with rational power and skill.
From the very beginning onward to the end, you divided this world into times, as was most fitting, in order, so that they both depart and come again.
You wisely move your own restless creatures according to your will, and you yourself remain very still and unchanging, forever and always.
There is none mightier and none more glorious, nor any equal to you throughout all creation, nor did you ever yet have any need of all the works that you have made;
but you made it all by your will, and by your own power you made the world and every creature, although there was no need at all for all those glorious things.
Great is the nature of your goodness, let whoever will reflect on it, for in every respect it is all one, you and your goodness.
It is your own, because nothing at all came to you from outside. I know well that your goodness, almighty Good, is wholly within yourself.
It is unlike our nature: everything good that we have on earth has come to us from outside, from God himself.
You did not take this on out of any envy, for nothing is like you, nor indeed is anything more all-skilful. For you, the all-good, devised it by your counsel alone, and then made them.
Before you there was no creature that made anything at all, but you, ruler of mankind, almighty God, made all things exceedingly good without any model; you yourself are the highest good.

Indeed, you, holy Father, Lord of hosts, created the world, this middle-earth, according to your will, by your powers, as you yourself wished, and by your will you rule all things; for you, true God, yourself give out every good thing.
For long ago you first created all creatures very much alike, yet in some ways unlike, and still you named them all together with one name: the world under the clouds.

Indeed, you, God of glory, Father, then divided that one name into four: one of these was earth, the second part of the world was water, fire is the third and air the fourth. That, put back together, is the whole world.
Yet the four have their original seats, each of them its own place, although each one is much mingled with the others,

and they are also bound fast together, peaceably and gently, by the power of the almighty Father and by your command, merciful Father, so that none of them dared to cross the boundary of another for fear of the Lord;
but the thanes, the king's warriors, are brought into harmony together, cold with heat and wet with dry, though they still strive against each other.
Water and earth bring forth fruits. Both are cold by nature: water is wet and cold. Earth, all-green, lies around the plains, and it too is cold.

Air is mixed, because it lives in the middle. It is no wonder that it is warm and cold, wet, the cloud's [?] ("tier"), blended with wind, because, as I have heard, it is in the middle, between fire and earth.
Many people know that fire is the highest of all created things, above the earth, and the ground is the lowest.
It is a wonder, Lord of hosts, that by your counsel you set boundaries for created things so wisely, and also mixed them together.
Lo, you firmly set the earth as a floor for the water, wet and cold, because otherwise the water, restless, weak and soft, would flow off widely in every direction.
I know well and truly that it could never stand by itself. But the earth holds it and also swallows part of it, so that afterwards, because of that soaking, the earth may be moistened [?] by the air.
Therefore leaves and grass spread throughout Britain, blooming and growing for the benefit of men. The cold earth brings forth many wonderful fruits, because it is moistened with water.
If that were not so, it would be dried to dust and then scattered far and wide by the wind, just as ashes are now often blown all over the earth.

Nothing could live on the earth, nor could any creature make use of water or dwell in it in any way, because of the cold alone, if you, King of angels, had not mixed some fire with the earth and the waters.
and by your skill you tempered cold and heat, so that the fire cannot burn the land and the sea-stream pale, though it is firmly joined with both, the Father's ancient work.
It seems to me no less a wonder that this earth and the sea, such cold creations, cannot by any means fully quench the fire that is lodged within them, joined there by the Lord's power.
That is the proper power of the sea-stream, of water and earth, and also in the clouds, and likewise up above the sky.
The proper first seat of fire, then, is its dwelling above all the other visible created things throughout this wide world.

Though it is mingled again with all the creatures of the world, yet it has no power to destroy any of them completely without the leave of him who granted us this life, that is, the eternal and almighty one.

Earth is heavier than the other creatures and more densely packed, because it has long stood lowest of all creatures, except the sky, which every day revolves around this spacious creation from outside,
Yet it never touches the earth, and it may not come nearer to it in one place than in another. It sweeps around it above and below, almost equally on each side.
Each created thing we are speaking about has its own separate dwelling place, yet it is also mixed with the others.
None of them can exist without the others.
They dwell together in a way that cannot clearly be seen. For example, earth and water dwell in fire, though every unwise person finds this hard to perceive. Yet these things are clear to the wise.
In the same way, fire is fixed in water and also in stones, held still and hard to see, but it is still there.
The Father of angels has bound that fire so firmly that it cannot go back to its homeland, where the other fire dwells, firmly settled, high above all this.
If the fire departs to its home, it at once leaves this transitory creation, overcome by cold. Yet every creature longs to go to the place where most of its kin are gathered together.
Glorious King of hosts, through your strong might you have wondrously established the earth so firmly that it leans to no side. It cannot sink this way or that any more than it always has.
Lo, though nothing earthly holds it up, it would be equally easy for this earth to fall upward or downward. It is most like what is in an egg: the yolk is in the middle, yet the egg glides around it.

So the whole world stands still in its place, with the streams around it, the tumult of the sea-floods, the airs and the stars, while the bright shell moves around it every day. It has done so for a long time.

Lo, God of peoples, you have set a threefold soul in us, and afterwards you also move and govern it through your strong might, so that there is no less of it in one little finger than there is in the whole body.
That is why I said clearly a little earlier that the soul of every man was a threefold creation. All philosophers say that one nature of every soul is anger, and the second is desire.
The third nature, reason, is better than the other two. That is no shameful faculty, for no beast has it, only humans.
Countless creatures have the other two; almost every beast has desires, and anger likewise.
Therefore men throughout the world have surpassed all earthly creatures, because they have what the others do not have: the one faculty that we named before.
Reason must always rule over desire in each one, and over anger likewise; with thought, with understanding, it must rule the man's whole mind.
It is the greatest power of a man's soul and the best of its particular skills.

Lo, you, Ruler of victories, glorious King of peoples, created the soul so that it should turn upon itself and around itself, just as the whole swift-running heaven does, swiftly circling this middle-earth each day by the Lord's power.
So does the soul of man: very like a wheel, it turns about itself, often pondering these earthly creations of the Lord by day and by night.
Sometimes it ponders, searching, about itself; sometimes again it ponders about the eternal God, its creator. It moves gliding, very like a wheel, and turns about itself.
When it ponders its creator with reason, it is raised up above itself, but it is wholly within itself when it ponders, searching, about itself;
it is very far beneath itself when it loves what is transitory and marvels at earthly things above eternal counsel.
Lo, you, eternal God, gave souls a dwelling in heaven, the best and most worthy of ample gifts, God almighty, according to the deserts of each one.
They all shine brightly in the heavens through the clear night, yet not all equally bright.
Lo, we often see on clear nights that the stars of heaven never all shine equally bright.
Lo, you, eternal God, also mingle heavenly things here with earth, souls with body; after that the earthly and the eternal dwell together, soul in flesh.
Lo, they always strive from here toward you; because they came here from you before, they must go back to you.
The body must keep its place afterwards on earth, because it grew from the earth before in the world.
They dwelt together just as long as was allowed them by the Almighty, who once joined them together; that is the true King,
who created this earth and then filled it with very diverse kinds of beasts, as I have heard, our Saviour.
Afterwards he sowed it with many seeds of trees and plants across the regions of the world.

Grant now, eternal God, to our minds that they may ascend up to you, Ruler of all creatures, through these hardships, and come to you from these troubles, gracious Father, Ruler of peoples; and that then, with the open eyes of our mind, they may,

through the abundance of your powers, see the source of all good things, which you yourself are, Lord of victory, God; and [make] the eyes of our mind whole, so that afterwards we may fasten them on you yourself.
Father of angels, drive away the thick mist that has now hung for a while before the eyes of our mind, heavy and dark.

Enlighten now the eyes of our mind with your light, Ruler of life, for you are the brightness of true light, gracious Father, and you yourself, Father almighty, are the firm resting-place of all the righteous.
Lo, you gently bring it about that they may see you yourself.
You, Ruler of peoples, are the beginning and the end of all things. Lo, you, Father of angels, bear all things easily, without toil.
You yourself are the way, and also the guide of every living one, and the beautiful place to which the way leads, toward which all men of the earth ever strive, to that glorious creation.
Well then, children of men throughout the world, let every free man strive toward the eternal good of which we speak, and toward the blessings that we tell of.
Whoever is now narrowly bound by useless love of this great world, let him quickly seek full freedom again, so that he may come forth to the blessings, the good of souls.
For that is the one rest from all toils, a hopeful harbour for the tall ships of our mind, a dwelling of calm sea.
That is the one haven that will always be calm after the waves of our toils, after every storm.
That is the sanctuary and the one comfort for all miseries after these worldly toils. That is a pleasant place to possess after these miseries.
But I know for certain that golden treasure, a silver jewel, any cunning gem, or the wealth of the world will never enlighten the eyes of the mind,
nor improve their sharpness at all for seeing true happiness. Instead, they blind the mind's eyes in every man's breast rather than make them brighter.
For everything that pleases in this present life is fleeting: earthly things that are always passing away.
But wondrous is that beauty and brightness that brightens the beauty of every creature and then rules over them all.
The Ruler does not want our souls to perish. He himself, the Ruler of life, will light them with his radiance.
If, then, any man can ever see with the clear eyes of his mind the pure brightness of heaven's light,
he will say that, compared with that great light of God Almighty, the brightness of the sun is darkness to every man. That light is eternal, without end, for every spirit, for blessed souls.

Whoever wants to search inwardly, rightly and with good judgement, so deeply that no man can scatter it and no earthly thing can spoil it, must first look within himself for what he had for some time been seeking around him.
Let him then seek it within his mind, and let him give up, as often as he can, every care that is useless to him, and let him gather, as fully as he can,
all his inner thought on that one thing. Let him tell his mind that it can find within itself everything it now so often and so constantly seeks outside itself: every good.
He will then see that all he had long kept in his inner chamber was evil and useless, just as clearly as he can look at the sun with his own eyes,
and he will also see that his inner thought is lighter and brighter than the sun's beam in summer, when the gem of the sky, the bright heavenly star, shines most clearly.
For the vices and heaviness of the body and its bad habits can never wholly draw righteousness out of the mind of any man;
Yet the sins, the heaviness and the vices of the body now often trouble every man's mind, most of all through evil forgetfulness.
With a mist of error it covers the sorrowing heart, the mind of every man, so that the mind cannot gleam and shine as brightly as it would if it had the power to.
yet some grain of the seed of truth is always kept in the soul, as long as the spirit dwells joined together with the body.
Still, the grain of that seed is always awakened by questioning, and afterwards also by good teaching, if it is to grow.
How can any man, a person with reason, find an answer about anything, even if someone questions him properly, if he has in his mind nothing, great or small, of righteousness or understanding?
Yet there is no man so entirely bereft of understanding that he cannot find any answer in his mind if he is asked.
So the old philosopher, our Plato, once told us a true saying. He said that anyone who has forgotten righteousness should quickly turn back into the memory of his mind.

There, in his secret chamber, in his spirit, he can then find righteousness firmly hidden. It is hidden above all by the daily turmoil of his mind, by the heaviness of his body, and by the cares that constantly stir in a man's breast and mind.
Lo, that man on earth is blessed in every way who can see the clearest, heaven-bright stream, the noble spring of every good, and can cast off from himself the dark mist, the darkness of the mind.
Yet, with God's help, we must still improve your inner thought with old and made-up fables, so that you may better find the right path up to the heavens, into the eternal home of our souls.
I have feathers swifter than a bird's, and with them I can fly far from the earth, over the high roof of this heaven. If I could now give feathers to the mind,
[?] your heart, with my feathers, until you could wholly despise this middle-earth and every earthly thing.
you could soar fittingly on feathers above the skies, wind your way far up over the clouds, and then look down from above over everything.
You could also pass over the fire that has long moved for many years between the air and the heavens, as the Father appointed for it in the beginning.
After that you could travel with the sun among the other stars.
After that you could very quickly be up in the sky, and then right away at the one star that is utterly cold,
which is the highest of all the stars. The sea-dwellers under the heavens call it Saturn. It is the cold, all-icy star, and it wanders highest, above all the other stars.
Then, once you have passed on beyond it, always going upward, you can go farther still. Soon after that you will be above the swiftly turning sky.

If you travel rightly, so that you leave the highest heaven behind you, then afterwards you may have your share of the true light, from where the one King reigns far and wide, up above the heavens and likewise below, over all creatures, and rules the world.
That is the wise King; that is he who rules over all the other kings of the earth throughout the nations of men, who with his bridle has bound the whole circuit of earth and heaven.
He handles his reins well, he who by his strong power always steers the swift chariot of heaven and earth.
That one judge is steadfast, unchanging, beautiful and glorious.
If you go by the right way up to that country, which is a noble place, even though you have now forgotten it, and if you ever come there again, then you will say and declare at once:
"This is wholly my own country, my home and native land. I came from here long ago, and I was born through the power of this Craftsman."
I will never wish to go out from here; rather I will always stand here firmly and at ease, by the Father's will."

If it then ever happens that you wish, or are obliged, to experience the darkness of the world again, you can easily see the unrighteous kings of the earth and the other proud, powerful men who treat this weary people worst,
that they are always very poor and powerless in everything, even those very ones whom this wretched people now for a while fears most.

Hear now a story about the proud, unrighteous kings of the earth. Here and now they shine wonderfully in many kinds of beautiful, bright garments, sitting on high seats close to the roof, adorned with gold and all kinds of gems, and surrounded by countless thanes and nobles.

These men are equipped with war-gear that shines in battle and are richly decked out with swords and sword-belts. They serve one another with great pomp, and with that pomp they all threaten the other neighbouring peoples on every side;
and the lord who rules the army has no regard for friend or foe, for life or possessions, but rushes savagely upon everyone, most like a mad dog;
he is too lifted up in his mind because of the power that each one of his glorious companions helps him to.
If someone then wanted to strip off him every piece of his royal clothing, and take from him the services and the power that he had before,
then you could see that he is very like one of the men who now crowd around him most eagerly to serve him. If he is not worse, I do not think he is any better.
If it should ever happen to him, unexpectedly, that he was deprived of the pomp and the clothing and the services and the power that we are speaking about,
if any of these were lost to him, I know that he would feel as if he had crept into a prison, or been [?] bound with chains.
I can explain that from excess in everything, in food and clothing, in wine-drinking and in sweetmeats, there grows most strongly the great madness of lust;
it greatly troubles the inner thought of every man's mind, and from it come most of the evils of arrogance and useless quarrels.
When they become enraged, the mind within their breast is beaten in the heart by the strong surge of hot temper, and soon afterwards it is also bound by sadness and held hard captive.
Then some hope begins to lie to him greatly about vengeance for that strife; his anger desires one thing and another; his recklessness promises him all of it and has no regard for what is right.
I told you earlier in this same book that every single one of the wide creatures always desired some good, according to its own ancient nature.
Unrighteous kings of the earth can never achieve anything good, because of the evil that I told you about before.
That is no wonder, because they always wish to subject themselves to each one of the vices that I named to you before.
He must then of necessity bow tightly to the captivity of those lords to whom he had earlier entirely subjected himself.
What is worse still is that he will not strive against that power at any time;
If he would only begin to fight back, and then keep up that fight, he would bear no guilt, even if he were overcome.
I can easily tell you, using old and fictional stories, a tale just like this very one that we two are speaking about.
It happened once, at a certain time, that Ulysses held two kingdoms under the emperor.
He was the ruler of the Thracian peoples and the guardian of the kingdom of Retia.
His overlord's name was well known among the people: Agamemnon, who ruled all the kingdom of the Greeks. It was widely known that at that time the Trojan War took place under the heavens.
The lord of the Greeks, hard in battle, went to seek the battlefield, and Ulysses with him. He led a hundred ships over the sea-stream, and sat there a long time, ten full winters.
When the time came that they had won that kingdom, the lord of the Greeks had paid dearly for the city of Troy with good companions.
When Ulysses, king of the Thracians, had leave to depart from there, he left behind him ninety-nine beaked ships.
From there he carried no more than one of the sea-steeds out onto the monster-haunted ocean, a foamy-sided, three-banked ship; that is the largest of Greek ships.

Then came cold weather, a fierce tumult of storms. The dark wave crashed against another and drove the band of warriors far out onto the Mediterranean, up onto the island where Apollo's daughter had lived for a great number of days.
This Apollo was of noble kin, the offspring of Jove, who was once a king.
He pretended to every man, small and great, that he was a god, the highest and holiest.
In this way the lord led the foolish people into error, until a countless number of people believed him, because he was by right the guardian of the kingdom and of their royal line.
It is widely known that at that time every nation held its lord to be the highest god, and worshipped him as the king of glory, if he had been rightly born to the kingdom.
The father of this Jove was a god as well, just as he was; the sea-dwellers, the children of men, called him Saturn. The peoples held each of them, one after another, to be the eternal god.
The nobly born daughter of Apollo was also supposed to be a goddess of the foolish people, of the warriors. She knew many incantations and practised sorcery.
She, a king's daughter, followed error more than anyone among many peoples. Among the hosts she was called Circe.
She ruled on the island to which Ulysses, king of the Thracians, came sailing with a single ship. The prince's journey was at once known to all the multitude that lived with her.

She loved the lord of the seafarers with boundless tenderness, and he likewise, with all his strength, loved her in his heart just as greatly. So he felt no desire in his mind for his homeland, beyond the young maiden.

Instead he lived with the woman after that, until none of his thanes could stay there with him any longer. Because of those miseries they longed for their homeland and meant to abandon their dear lord.

Then the peoples began to make up tales. They said that with her magic she would transform men, and with cruel, baleful arts cast the king's thanes into the bodies of wild beasts, and afterwards fetter them, and bind many with chains as well.
Some became wolves and could not then bring forth words, but from time to time began to howl.
Some were boars, and always grunted when they had to lament some pain.
Those who were lions began to roar hideously in anger whenever they had to call out to the company.
The men, old and young, were all turned into some beast, whichever one each had most resembled in his lifetime, except the king, whom the queen loved.
None of the others would taste human food; they loved the way of life of beasts more, though it was not fitting.
They had no more likeness to men, the dwellers on earth, than their inward thought. Each one had his own mind, but it was heavily bound with sorrows because of the hardships that weighed on them.
Lo, the foolish men who long believed in these sorceries, these false tales, still knew that no one can change the mind and understanding by sorcery.
Even though she could bring it about that their bodies were changed for a long time. That is a wonderful, great power that every mind has over the transitory and sluggish body.
From such things as these you can clearly see that the skills and powers of the body come from the mind, for every man, each single one.
You can easily perceive that a vice of the mind harms every man more than the infirmity of the transitory body.

None among the people need expect the outcome that the weary flesh could ever wholly turn the mind of any man to itself. Rather, the vices of each mind and the inner thought of each man lead the body wherever it wishes.
Why must you always trouble your minds with unjust hatreds, as the waves of the sea-flood stir the ice-cold sea and toss it before the wind? Why do you blame your fate, which has no power?
Why can you not wait for the death, bitter by nature, that the Lord has ordained for you, now that it hastens toward you every day?
Can you not see that it is always on the track of every offspring of the earth, beasts and birds alike?
In the same way Death, the terrible hunter, is always on the hunt after mankind throughout this world. He will never abandon any track until he catches what he was tracking a while before.

It is a wretched thing that city-dwellers, unhappy men, cannot wait for him; they want to shoot first, ahead of him, like the race of birds or wild beasts. They fight among themselves, and each would kill the other.
But it is wrong for any man to hate another in his heart with malicious thoughts, as a bird or a beast does. It would be most right for each man to give the other a just reward,
[?] … work according to their deeds to the dwellers in the world in every matter; that is, that he should love every good person as eagerly as he can, and have mercy on the wicked, as we said before.
He must love the man in his heart, and hate all his vices and cut them away as much as he can.

Who among the unlearned on earth now does not wonder at the motion of the clouds, the swiftness of the sky and the course of the stars, and how every day they turn around the whole world from outside?
Who among mankind does not wonder at these beautiful stars, and how some have a much shorter orbit while others travel a longer way around all this?

People in the world call one of these constellations the Wain's shafts. They have a shorter path and course, and a smaller orbit, than other stars, because they turn around the axis from outside, circling close to its northern end.
The whole wide sky turns on that same axis. It glides quickly, sweeping toward the south, swift and untiring.
Who in the world does not marvel, except only those who knew it already, that many a star has a greater orbit in the heavens, and at times again travels a smaller one,

those that move about the end of the axle, or those that travel much more widely, rushing mightily around its middle? One of these is called Saturn, which takes about thirty years by count to go around the world.
Boötes, another star, also shines brightly. In the same way it comes back after a count of thirty years to the same place where it was before.
Who among people in the world does not marvel at how some stars travel down to the sea, under the ocean currents, as it seems to people?
In the same way some think that the sun does this, but that belief is no truer at all.
The sun is no nearer the ocean in the evening or early morning than at midday. Yet it seems to people that it goes into the sea and moves under the water when it glides down to its setting.
Who in the world does not wonder at the full moon when, under the clouds, it is suddenly robbed of its beauty and covered with darkness?
And what man might not also marvel at each star: why do they not shine in clear weather in front of the sun, as they always do at midnight in front of the moon, in a bright sky?
Look, many people now wonder greatly at this and that, yet do not wonder that every creature, people and beasts alike, keeps up great, useless and constant hostility toward one another.

It is a strange thing that they do not wonder how it often thunders violently in the clouds and then stops again for a time, and likewise how the wave always struggles against the land, and the wind against the wave.

Who wonders at this, or again at another thing: why ice can come from water? Then the beautiful, bright sun shines hot in the sky, and soon the lovely icy pool turns back to its own nature and becomes water.
No one thinks it a great wonder when he can see something every day. Foolish people wonder more at what they see more rarely, though every wise person thinks it a much smaller wonder in his mind.

Unsteady people always think that something in the ancient creation they seldom see never existed before. Even more, worldly men think it came about by chance as a new happening if it never appeared to any of them before. That is a wretched thing.
But if any of them ever becomes so eager to know that he begins to learn many arts, and the Guardian of life tears from his mind the great foolishness that had long remained in it and covered it,
then I know well that they will not wonder at many things that now seem astonishing and wonderful to people everywhere.

If you now wish to understand eagerly, with a clear mind, the high power of the Lord of the world, give heed with all your might to the stars of heaven: how they keep constant peace among themselves, and have done so for a long time.
The Prince of glory set this custom for them at the creation, so that the fiery sun may not seek the path of the snow-cold one, the boundaries of the moon.
Look, neither of those great heavenly bodies ever touches the other's course before the other has moved away.

Nor indeed will the star that wise men call Ursa go down into the western part of the sky. All the stars sink after the sun, together with the sky, beneath the ground of the earth, but it alone stands still.
That is no wonder: it is wonderfully fixed near the upper end of the sky's axis.

Then there is a star, bright above the others, that comes up from the east before the sun. The children of men under the heavens call it the morning star, because it announces day to people throughout the towns. After it, the sun, bright as the sky, brings day to everyone together.

The forerunner is fair and beautiful. It comes up from the east ahead of the sun, and again after the sun it glides to its setting, west under the world. The nations of men change its name when night comes: they all call it the evening star.
It is swifter than the sun. After they go down to their setting, the noble star outruns the sun, until it appears to men in the east again before the sun.
By the Lord's might the noble stars, the sun and the moon, have divided day and night evenly between them, in close harmony, as the Father ordained for them at the beginning.
You need not think that the beautiful stars will grow weary of that service before Judgment Day. After that the Creator of mankind will do with them as seems fitting to him.

Therefore almighty God does not leave them alone on one half of this heaven, lest they destroy other noble creatures. Instead, the eternal God moderates all the wide creation and gently brings it into harmony.
Sometimes the dry drives out the wet. Sometimes, by the Creator's skill, he mixes cold with heat. Sometimes the all-bright flame, light in the air, turns back again to the sky above.
Behind it lies a heavy portion of the ground, though for a while before, the cold earth had held and hidden it within herself by the might of the Holy One.

By the King's command it comes every year: the earth brings forth every kind of offspring, and every year the hot summer prepares and dries seed and fruit for the children of men across the wide ground, and harvest hands the ripe crops to the people who dwell here.
After that, rain, and likewise hail and snow, moisten the ground in wintertime, in fierce weather.
Therefore the earth receives all seeds and makes them grow every year; in springtime the leaves sprout up.

But the gracious Lord feeds the children of men on earth with all that grows, the fruits of the world. The Ruler of the heavens brings it forth well when he wishes, and shows it again to the dwellers on earth; the saving God takes it away when he wishes.
And the highest Good, the King himself, sits on a high throne, and this wide creation serves and attends him. From there he rules the creatures of the world with reins.
That is no wonder: he is the God of hosts, King and Lord of every living thing, wellspring and origin of all creatures, maker and creator of this world, the wisdom and law of the world's inhabitants.
He sends all creatures out from here on his errands and commands them to come back.
If he had not established all creatures so firmly, every one of them would have to be harshly scattered; every one of them would come entirely to nothing, harshly dissolved.
yet all the creatures of heaven and earth share one love in common: that they serve such a Lord of peoples and rejoice that their Father rules.
That is no wonder, because no creature could ever survive otherwise if it did not serve its origin, the glorious Lord, with all its might.
Homer lived in the east among the Greeks and was the most skilled of poets in that nation. He was the friend and teacher of Virgil, the best of masters to that famous poet.
Lo, that Homer often and repeatedly praised the beauty of the sun greatly, and often and repeatedly told people of its noble powers in songs and stories.
Yet even though it is clear and bright, it cannot shine anywhere near all created things. And even the created things it can shine on, it cannot light up all together, both inside and out.
But the almighty Ruler and Maker of the world's creatures looks over all his own work and sees through all creatures together.
That is rightly the true sun, about whom we may sing such things without falsehood.

Lo, you can perceive, if you care to think about it, that many creatures move across the earth in various and different ways. They have colour and motion, both unlike, and forms of many kinds, known and unknown.
They creep and crawl with their whole body touching the earth. They have no help from wings, nor can they walk on feet; they make use of the earth as was granted to them.
Some tread the ground on two feet, some on four, and some fly and wheel beneath the clouds.
Yet every creature is bent toward the ground, droops downward, looks at the world, and longs for the earth, some out of necessity, some out of greed.
Man alone among the Lord's creatures walks with his face upright.
This signifies that his faith and his mind's thought should be directed more upward to the heavens than downward, so that he does not turn his mind downward like a beast.
It is not fitting that any man's mind should be bent downward while his face is turned upward!
